question: Consider the SSL method described as: 'Introduces a queue of negative samples to decouple the number of negative samples from the batch size.' Which SSL algorithm does this correspond to?
options: A) MoCo (Momentum Contrast)
B) SimCLR
C) BYOL
D) Barlow Twins
explanation: MoCo maintains a dynamic dictionary as a queue of encoded keys, so the number of negatives is decoupled from the mini-batch size. SimCLR, by contrast, depends on a large batch for negatives.

question: Which SSL method is best described as 'the contrastive version of the SplitBrain Autoencoder', using two views (e.g. different channels/modalities of the same scene) with a contrastive objective?
options: A) SimCLR
B) BYOL
C) CMC (Contrastive Multiview Coding)
D) SimSiam
explanation: CMC generalizes SplitBrain by replacing the reconstruction loss with a contrastive objective across multiple views/channels of the same scene.

question: Which SSL algorithm is: 'Similar to SimCLR but does not need negative samples, and introduces an EMA (Exponential Moving Average) target network'?
options: A) MoCo
B) BYOL (Bootstrap Your Own Latent)
C) Barlow Twins
D) SimSiam
explanation: BYOL uses an online network and an EMA target network; the online predictor is trained to match the target representation, removing the need for negatives.

question: Which SSL algorithm 'uses a projector after the encoder to increase the dimensionality of the representation to apply a cross-correlation loss' that pushes the empirical cross-correlation matrix between two augmented views toward the identity?
options: A) SimCLR
B) SimSiam
C) Barlow Twins
D) MoCo v3
explanation: Barlow Twins enforces the cross-correlation matrix between embeddings of two distorted views to be close to the identity (redundancy reduction); a high-dim projector makes the loss effective.

question: Compared to traditional variational inference (optimizing $q_\phi$ individually per $x_i$), amortized inference (one encoder for all $x$) generally has what property?
options: A) Per-example inference achieves a lower or equal KL than the shared amortized encoder.
B) Amortized inference always achieves strictly lower KL than per-example inference.
C) Amortized and per-example inference achieve exactly the same KL.
D) Amortized inference removes the approximation gap entirely.
explanation: Sharing a single encoder across all data points introduces an amortization gap, so the expected KL is at least as large as under per-example optimal $q^*_i$.

question: In a VAE, one way to reduce the amortization gap (while leaving the approximation gap unchanged) is to:
options: A) Increase the capacity of the encoder network parameterizing $q_\phi(z\mid x)$.
B) Decrease the weight of the KL$(q_\phi(z\mid x)\|p(z))$ term in the objective.
C) Include a GAN-like adversarial term.
D) Use IAF in the encoder to model non-factorial distributions.
explanation: A larger encoder can produce closer-to-optimal $q$ for each $x$ without changing the variational family (which would affect the approximation gap).

question: You are training an LLM with RLHF and want the REINFORCE estimator to maximize $\mathbb{E}_{\hat s\sim p_\theta}[R(\hat s)]$. Which expression correctly gives the gradient?
options: A) $\mathbb{E}_{\hat s\sim p_\theta}[R(\hat s)\nabla_\theta\log p_\theta(\hat s)]$
B) $\nabla_\theta R(\hat s)$ for any sampled $\hat s$
C) $\mathbb{E}_{\hat s\sim p_\theta}[\nabla_\theta R(\hat s)]$
D) $\mathbb{E}_{\hat s\sim p_\theta}[\log R(\hat s)\nabla_\theta p_\theta(\hat s)]$
explanation: Standard score-function / log-derivative identity used when $R$ is not differentiable in $\theta$.

question: Which three-step pipeline is used in InstructGPT to fine-tune a language model?
options: A) (1) Supervised fine-tuning on human demonstrations; (2) train a reward model from human preference comparisons (Bradley-Terry); (3) RL fine-tuning (PPO) of the policy against the reward model.
B) (1) Unsupervised pretraining; (2) contrastive learning on token pairs; (3) distillation into a smaller model.
C) (1) Train a reward model from scratch; (2) supervised fine-tuning; (3) adversarial fine-tuning.
D) (1) RLHF first; (2) then supervised fine-tuning; (3) then pretraining from scratch.
explanation: InstructGPT: SFT on demonstrations, then a reward model trained from human preference rankings (Bradley-Terry), then policy optimization against that reward model via PPO.

question: Why is the Bradley-Terry paired comparison model used for training the RLHF reward model?
options: A) It regresses absolute scores directly.
B) Humans rank pairs more reliably than giving absolute scores; Bradley-Terry converts pairwise preferences into a consistent scalar reward.
C) It removes the need for any human labels.
D) It ensures the reward model is invertible.
explanation: Pairwise preferences are more reliable; Bradley-Terry parameterizes $P(a\succ b)=\sigma(r(a)-r(b))$, letting a latent scalar reward be learned from comparisons.

question: In PixelCNN, mask type A zeroes the current pixel and all 'future' pixels in the kernel, while mask type B keeps the current pixel. To ensure a valid autoregressive receptive field, which combination is required between the first and subsequent conv layers?
options: A) Mask A for the first layer, mask B for all subsequent layers.
B) Mask B for the first layer, mask A for all subsequent layers.
C) Mask A for every layer.
D) Mask B for every layer.
explanation: The first layer must use mask A so output at pixel $i$ doesn't depend on input pixel $i$. Deeper layers can use mask B because the feature at position $i$ already excludes information about input pixel $i$.

question: You are designing a normalizing-flow generative model. Which two properties must the neural network have?
options: A) It must be differentiable and invertible, with a tractable Jacobian determinant.
B) It must be non-invertible but have a tractable Hessian.
C) It must be a contraction mapping with Lipschitz constant less than 1.
D) It must be stochastic and have a tractable variance.
explanation: Change-of-variables requires invertible differentiable maps with a tractable log-determinant of the Jacobian; otherwise exact likelihood is infeasible.

question: WGAN with critic $D(x;\psi_0,\psi_1)=\psi_0(x+2)^2+\psi_1(x-1)^2$ to match $\mathbb{P}=\delta_0$ from $\mathbb{Q}=\delta_1$, under Lipschitz-1 constraint. Which $(\psi_0,\psi_1)$ maximizes the critic's objective?
options: C) Values that saturate the Lipschitz-1 constraint so that $D$ has slope $\pm 1$ on $[0,1]$ — e.g. $(-1/6, 1/6)$.
D) Any $(\psi_0,\psi_1)$ with $|\psi_0|+|\psi_1|>1$.
explanation: Under Lipschitz-1 and the dual form of $W_1$, the optimal critic is a 1-Lipschitz function proportional to signed distance between supports; $(\psi_0,\psi_1)=(-1/6,1/6)$ saturates the constraint and maximizes the objective.

question: A known problem with self-attention in very deep Transformers is that softmax can concentrate mass on a few tokens. Which statement correctly describes the issue AND a standard remedy?
options: A) Deep Transformers suffer vanishing gradients because dot products become too small; fix by increasing key dimension.
B) Softmax can concentrate attention on a few tokens, ignoring the rest; mitigated by multi-head attention, which attends to multiple subspaces.
C) Attention weights become uniform with depth; fix by reducing softmax temperature.
D) Fixed positional encodings lose information; fix by using relative positional encodings.
explanation: Multi-head attention provides multiple independent attention patterns in different subspaces, reducing the risk of a single softmax over-concentrating on a few tokens.

question: What is the key advantage of relative positional embeddings over absolute ones in Transformers?
options: A) They eliminate the fixed-length requirement on input sequences.
B) They reduce attention complexity from quadratic to linear.
C) They reduce the dimensionality of positional representations.
D) They generalize better to variable-length and shifted contexts by encoding position differences.
explanation: Relative encodings depend on $i-j$ rather than absolute $i$, so the same relationships generalize across shifts and longer sequences not seen at training time.

question: Which statement correctly explains a fundamental advantage of Transformer-XL over standard Transformers?
options: A) It caches hidden states across segment boundaries via a recurrence, enabling long-range dependencies without recomputing prior-segment attention.
B) It uses a fixed-length context window per segment.
C) It reduces input dimensionality via relative position encodings.
D) It reduces self-attention to linear complexity by truncating the attention matrix.
explanation: Transformer-XL caches hidden states from the previous segment (with relative positions), giving longer effective context without recomputing attention over earlier tokens.

question: Why is LoRA frequently used when fine-tuning LLMs with RLHF?
options: A) LoRA increases expressive power by adding many trainable parameters.
B) LoRA restricts updates to a low-rank subspace, enabling efficient fine-tuning while preserving pre-trained capabilities.
C) LoRA incorporates preference scores directly into the parameterization.
D) LoRA replaces policy-gradient, making RLHF redundant.
explanation: LoRA freezes base weights and learns small low-rank factors $A,B$ so $\Delta W=AB^\top$; much less memory/compute, and most of the pretrained backbone is preserved.

question: Which statement correctly captures a key difference between SimCLR and BYOL?
options: A) Both require explicit negative pairs; BYOL uses a momentum encoder.
B) Both use symmetric contrastive losses; BYOL adds a temperature parameter.
C) SimCLR uses a momentum encoder; BYOL uses batch normalization to avoid collapse.
D) SimCLR uses negative pairs in the contrastive loss; BYOL does not — it aligns online and target networks without negatives.
explanation: SimCLR is contrastive (positives vs negatives). BYOL avoids negatives entirely, predicting the target (EMA) network's representation from the online network.

question: In a DDPM with forward process $q(x_t|x_{t-1})=\mathcal{N}(x_t;\sqrt{1-\beta_t}x_{t-1},\beta_t I)$, which statement about the reverse $p_\theta(x_{t-1}|x_t)$ is true?
options: A) It is deterministic to ensure exact inversion of the forward process.
B) It is modeled as a Gaussian with learned mean and fixed variance.
C) It must condition on all $x_0,\dots,x_{t-1}$.
D) It shares parameters with the forward process for symmetry.
explanation: For small $\beta_t$, the true reverse conditional is approximately Gaussian; DDPM parameterizes $p_\theta(x_{t-1}|x_t)=\mathcal{N}(x_{t-1};\mu_\theta,\sigma_t^2 I)$ with fixed schedule variance.

question: The DDPM ELBO uses $q(x_{t-1}|x_t,x_0)$ as a per-step target. Which best describes how this enables training?
options: A) It matches reverse outputs to data via a reconstruction loss.
B) It maximizes the likelihood of each noise sample independently.
C) It approximates the posterior over $x_{t-1}$ using $x_t,x_0$, and penalizes deviation of the learned reverse from it.
D) It computes the JSD between forward and reverse trajectories.
explanation: $q(x_{t-1}|x_t,x_0)$ is a tractable Gaussian target, and the KL at each step trains $p_\theta(x_{t-1}|x_t)$ to match it.

question: Modern DDPMs reparameterize the reverse process as noise prediction — given $x_t=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\epsilon$, the network predicts $\epsilon$. Why is this advantageous?
options: A) It allows cross-entropy loss instead of KL divergence.
B) It avoids computing forward-process variance.
C) Predicting $\epsilon$ yields a simple tractable MSE objective that aligns with the variational bound.
D) It decouples denoising from generation, enabling parallel sampling.
explanation: Reparameterizing the mean in terms of predicted noise turns the per-step KL into a simple weighted MSE matching the ELBO up to known weights.

question: Consider a single-step RL problem with policy $\pi_\theta(a)=e^{\theta a}/\sum_{a'}e^{\theta a'}$, $\mathcal A=\{1,2\}$, rewards $R(1)=4$, $R(2)=8$. Using REINFORCE, what is $\nabla_\theta J(\theta)$?
options: A) $\dfrac{4e^\theta+8e^{2\theta}}{(e^\theta+e^{2\theta})^2}$
B) $\dfrac{4e^\theta+16e^{3\theta}}{(e^\theta+e^{2\theta})^3}$
C) $\dfrac{4e^{3\theta}}{(e^\theta+e^{2\theta})^2}$
D) $\dfrac{4e^\theta(e^\theta+2e^{2\theta})}{(e^\theta+e^{2\theta})^2}$
explanation: Direct computation yields $4e^{3\theta}/(e^\theta+e^{2\theta})^2$.

question: In a modified CLIP setup, we contrast joint embedding $f(I,T)$ with a text-only embedding $g(T)$. To avoid both collapse AND the degenerate solution where $f$ ignores $I$, which sampling strategy works?
options: A) Positives: $(f(I_i,T_i), g(T_i))$; Negatives: $(f(I_i,T_{j\ne i}), g(T_{j\ne i}))$.
B) Positives: $(f(I_i,T_i), f(I_j,T_j))$; Negatives: $(g(T_i), g(T_j))$.
C) Positives: $(f(I_i,T_i), g(T_i))$; Negatives: $(g(T_i), g(T_j))$.
D) Positives: $(f(I_i,T_j), g(T_i))$ with $I_j\sim I_i$; Negatives: $(f(I_i,T_{j\ne i}), g(T_{j\ne i}))$.
explanation: Using in-batch mismatched image-text pairs $(I_i,T_{j\ne i})$ as negatives forces $f$ to depend on $I$; contrasting $g(T_{j\ne i})$ prevents collapse to a constant embedding.

question: Normalizing flows require an invertible map $g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$. Which candidate(s) are invertible on $(-\infty,\infty)$? (i) $g(z)=af(bz+c)$, $f=\mathrm{ReLU}$, $a,b>0$; (ii) $g(z)=\sigma^{-1}(\sum_i w_i\sigma(a_iz+b_i))$ with $0<w_i<1$, $\sum w_i=1$, $a_i>0$; (iii) $g(z)=z+\mathrm{ReLU}(bz+c)$.
options: A) Only (i)
B) Only (ii)
C) (ii) and (iii) only
D) All three
explanation: (i) fails: ReLU is constant on negatives. (ii) sum of strictly increasing sigmoids with positive weights, composed with strictly increasing $\sigma^{-1}$ — invertible. (iii) derivative $\ge 1$ — invertible.

question: To estimate the variational gap using $K$ i.i.d. samples from $q_\phi(z|x)$ on a test set, which expression gives a valid practical estimate (IWAE bound minus single-sample ELBO)?
options: A) $\log\big[\tfrac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^K\tfrac{p(x,z_k)}{q_\phi(z_k|x)}\big]-\tfrac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^K\big[\log p(x,z_k)-\log q_\phi(z_k|x)\big]$
B) $\log\big[\tfrac{1}{K}\sum_k\tfrac{p(x,z_k)}{q_\phi(z_k|x)}\big]$ alone.
C) $\log\big[\tfrac{1}{K}\sum_k\tfrac{p(z_k|x)}{q_\phi(z_k|x)}\big]$
D) None of these
explanation: The IWAE estimator $\log\tfrac{1}{K}\sum p(x,z_k)/q(z_k|x)$ is a tighter lower bound on $\log p(x)$ than the single-sample ELBO; the difference estimates the variational gap.
